metaDescription: Six handheld mandoline slicers compared on guard design, stability, thickness settings and storage, for even slices without a bulky countertop unit.
introParagraphs: A handheld mandoline gives you the even, paper-thin slices of a full-size slicer without the counter space, but it hands the safety job to you. The blade is exposed, the food moves under your hand, and the guard or holder is the only thing between your fingertips and the edge. That is why the guard and the grip matter more here than any spec on the box.

This comparison covers six handheld slicers with different safety ideas: the OXO with a stable foot and a hook for a bowl, the OXO Precision with a self-adjusting holder, the Joseph Joseph with three grip styles, the Fullstar with steel-tipped guard prongs, the Ibergrif with a blade lock, and the compact ZKIRON with a thumb slider.

We judged each from product specs and buyer feedback, not bench cutting. Use the safety notes as seriously as the thickness numbers, and pair any of these with a cut-resistant glove if you slice often.

products.name: OXO Good Grips Handheld Mandoline Slicer
products.description:
The OXO is the safest-feeling slicer in the group because it does the basics well. A large non-slip handle gives a confident hold, and a stable foot keeps the base from sliding around when the stroke gets firm.

Three thickness settings, 1 mm, 2.5 mm and 4 mm, cover most jobs: thin cucumbers for salad, medium potatoes for gratin, thick cuts for chips. You can slice directly onto a plate, on a board, or hook it over a bowl so the pieces drop where you want them.

It offers only three settings, so there is no julienne or fine dial like the Fullstar's extras. It also needs a steady hand on the food, which means a guard or a glove is wise. If you want one reliable slicer without a learning curve, this is it. Compared with the ZKIRON at 3 mm maximum, it reaches 4 mm for thicker potato rounds, and the hook-over-bowl feature means you can slice while standing at the sink with almost no cleanup.
products.bestFor: Cooks who want a stable, simple slicer with a confident grip.

products.name: OXO Good Grips Precision Handheld Mandoline
products.description:
The Precision is built around its holder. An automatic, height-adjustable food holder applies even pressure as the food shrinks, so your fingers stay farther from the blade for more of the stroke.

Five cutting options, including julienne and thin cuts, make it more versatile than the three-setting OXO. The slim body leaves counter space free, and the holder stores neatly with the slicer instead of wandering off.

Soft produce can slip out of the holder, and the holder adds a part to wash and dry. Handheld use also needs a steady board underneath. It is the pick when the guard is your priority. Compared with the Fullstar at four settings, you get one more cutting style but a more elaborate holder to wash, so budget a minute at the sink after each use. Dry the holder fully before storing it with the body.

products.name: Joseph Joseph Multi-Grip Hand-held Mandoline
products.description:
Joseph Joseph answers the guard question with versatility. Its precision food grip comes in three styles: a pinch grip for small items, a center grip for round slices and a flat grip for longer slices.

That lets you match the guard to the food instead of forcing every vegetable into one holder. The tool also offers three slice thicknesses and adjustable blades, so the base setup is similar to the OXO at three settings.

The tradeoff is complexity. More grips mean more pieces to choose from and clean, and the listing gives few specifics beyond the grip names. It is a smart choice if you slice mixed shapes, from onions to carrots to lemons. Against the Ibergrif holder that adapts poorly to odd shapes, the three-style grip is the clearer answer, though both stop at three thickness settings. Practice the pinch grip on a small onion before you rely on it for a full prep session.

products.name: Fullstar Handheld Mandoline Slicer and Julienne Cutter
products.description:
The Fullstar offers four thickness settings at 1 mm, 2 mm, 3 mm and 4 mm, one more than the OXO, and a built-in julienne blade that turns it into a two-in-one tool. For salads and slaws, that range is genuinely useful.

The guard carries stainless steel tips, which the maker contrasts with plastic prongs on cheaper competitors. Steel tips grip produce better, though they are still a guard rather than a glove.

It is a bulkier choice than the slim OXO Precision and has more parts to wash. Keep it on the list if julienne matters; skip it if you only slice cucumbers. Wash the julienne blade with a brush, and slide the guard on before you reach for the next vegetable. Next to the OXO at 2.5 mm, its 2 mm and 3 mm steps give finer control for coleslaw and thin potato work.

products.name: Ibergrif Handheld Mandoline Slicer
products.description:
Ibergrif brings a blade safety lock to the table, which secures the edge for storage and cleaning. That solves the risky moments outside of slicing, when a bare blade in a drawer or sink is most dangerous.

A food holder is included for fingertip distance, and the non-slip design with three thickness settings suits salads, chips and everyday prep. It is compact enough for a small drawer.

The build is lighter, so more of the control rests on your own technique. The holder adapts poorly to odd-shaped produce, and there are only three settings. Choose it when storage safety is the concern. It is the most drawer-friendly of the three-setting models, since the lock means the edge is covered whenever you are not slicing, and it needs no extra sleeve or case. Pair it with a cut-resistant glove if you slice firm squash.

products.name: ZKIRON Adjustable Handheld Mandoline Slicer
products.description:
ZKIRON is the compact choice. A thumb slider moves between 1 mm, 2 mm and 3 mm with no blade swap, which cuts down on handling an exposed blade.

The included hand guard grips produce between two spiked contact surfaces, and the maker says to use it from the first slice. That is good advice, since a guard only helps when it is on the food before the stroke starts.

It is sized for small to medium produce like cucumbers, onions, potatoes, carrots, zucchini, radishes and lemons. Settings stop at 3 mm, so thick cuts are out. Pick it for light daily slicing. Next to the Ibergrif, which also offers three settings, the slider avoids any blade handling during changes, which reduces the riskiest moment of use. Keep the guard on the produce through the whole stroke, not just the first pass.

buyingCriteria.explanation: The guard decides how close your fingers get to the blade. The OXO Precision adjusts its holder height automatically, the Joseph Joseph offers three grip styles, and the Fullstar uses steel-tipped prongs. A guard that does not hold the produce is worse than none, so choose one that fits your usual vegetables. Use it from the first slice, as ZKIRON also advises.

Range matters for salads and slaws. The Fullstar offers four settings from 1 mm to 4 mm, the OXO offers 1, 2.5 and 4 mm, and the ZKIRON covers 1 to 3 mm. A tool that tops out at 3 mm cannot make thick potato chips. Pick the range that matches your most common recipe.

A slicer that slides mid-stroke is dangerous. The OXO Good Grips pairs a large non-slip handle with a stable foot, and the Ibergrif is designed with a non-slip body. Place a damp cloth under the board, and check that the handle suits the size of your hand.

Most accidents happen while washing or storing the blade. The Ibergrif has a blade safety lock, and the OXO Precision stores its holder with the body. Wash with a brush rather than a sponge held against the edge, and never leave a bare blade in a sink of soapy water.

Julienne and thin cuts widen what the tool can do. The Fullstar has a built-in julienne blade and the OXO Precision offers five cutting options. If you only slice, these extras add edges to handle without adding value, so pick them for a clear reason.

Small slicers fit small produce. The ZKIRON targets small to medium vegetables, and the Ibergrif holder adapts poorly to odd shapes. Large onions or wide potatoes may not fit. Choose by the biggest thing you will slice regularly. If that is a large onion or a wide potato, trim it flat on one side first so it sits square in the holder, and expect a compact slicer to take two passes on something big.

howWeEvaluated.title: Guard effectiveness
howWeEvaluated.description: We evaluated how well each guard or holder keeps fingers clear. The OXO Precision leads with an automatic height-adjustable holder, and the Joseph Joseph is strong with three grip styles. A guard that slips on soft produce loses points.

howWeEvaluated.title: Stability and handling
howWeEvaluated.description: Handles, feet and body weight were compared from product specs and buyer feedback. The OXO Good Grips earns credit for its large handle and stable foot, while lighter builds such as the Ibergrif push more control onto the user.

howWeEvaluated.title: Thickness range
howWeEvaluated.description: We counted settings and spread. The Fullstar leads with four, from 1 mm to 4 mm, while the OXO covers 1, 2.5 and 4 mm and the ZKIRON stops at 3 mm. More range scores higher when it is easy to change.

howWeEvaluated.title: Storage and cleaning safety
howWeEvaluated.description: Blade locks, stored holders and tool-free adjustment reduce risky handling. The Ibergrif has a blade lock and the ZKIRON uses a slider with no blade swap. Fewer exposed edges scored higher.

howWeEvaluated.title: Versatility and fit
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared cut options and produce size limits. The Fullstar and OXO Precision add julienne and extra cuts, while the ZKIRON suits small produce only. The lineup positions the OXO as the all-rounder and the OXO Precision as the safety pick.

howToChoose.intro: Two ways to protect your hand.

cards.label: Holder
cards.text: A holder keeps fingertips away by gripping the food. The OXO Precision, Joseph Joseph, Ibergrif and ZKIRON include one. Pick a holder if you slice firm produce and want built-in distance.

cards.label: Cut-resistant glove
cards.text: A glove protects the hand directly and lets you slice awkward or slippery items without a holder. It works with every slicer here, including the OXO Good Grips. Pick a glove for soft produce and extra safety.

faq.a: They can be safe with the right habits. Use the guard from the first slice, keep a damp cloth under the board, and make short, steady strokes. A cut-resistant glove adds protection, especially for slippery or oddly shaped food. Never rush, and stop slicing when the piece gets too small to hold safely. Use a knife for the last stub rather than pushing it across the blade.

faq.q: How do I clean a mandoline blade safely?
faq.a: Use a brush or a long-handled sponge and keep fingers away from the edge. The Ibergrif has a blade lock for storage and cleaning, and the OXO Precision stores its holder with the body. Rinse after each use so residue does not dry. Hold the slicer by its handle with the blade facing away from you, and let it air-dry on a rack. Do not toss it into a sink of soapy water where the edge is hidden.

For salads and cucumbers, 1 to 2 mm. For potatoes, 2.5 to 4 mm. The Fullstar offers 1, 2, 3 and 4 mm, the OXO offers 1, 2.5 and 4 mm, and the ZKIRON stops at 3 mm. Choose by your usual recipe. Thinner slices cook faster and crisp better, while thicker ones hold their shape in a bake. A setting you rarely use is wasted, so a simple three-step slicer often beats a fancier one.

faq.q: Do I really need the guard?
faq.a: Yes, or a glove. The guard keeps your fingertips away from the edge, but only if you use it from the first slice. Soft produce may slip out of some holders, so switch to a glove in that case. Holders also work best when they press straight down, so keep the food square to the blade. If the holder feels loose on a particular vegetable, slow down or choose another cut method.

A smooth surface and wet hands are the usual causes. Put a damp cloth under the board and check for a stable foot, like the one on the OXO Good Grips. A non-slip handle also helps. Dry the handle and your hands before you start, and rest the lower edge against a bowl or board lip if you are slicing onto a counter. A slicer that slides more than a few millimeters is a warning sign to stop and reset.

faq.q: Is a handheld better than a countertop slicer?
faq.a: It depends on space. A handheld stores in a drawer and hooks over a bowl, but it relies on your hand control. A countertop slicer is larger but often more stable. Choose by kitchen size and comfort. For a household that slices a few times a week, a handheld is usually enough, and it avoids the blade cassettes and large guards that bigger machines carry. If you prep for a crowd, step up to a larger unit.

faq.q: Can I slice soft foods like tomatoes?
faq.a: Only with a very sharp blade and light pressure. Soft produce can slip out of holders, as noted for the OXO Precision. Firm produce is the safer choice for any handheld mandoline. Chill soft items first so they hold their shape, and slice with short strokes rather than forcing the food across the edge. A dull blade makes soft produce worse, so replace tired slicers.
